segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went over the side at first light with two days left, all three of them, and Walter Ames sat in the stern of Maud's boat holding the oars he had been told not to use. Jory Brennick carried the pry bar on a loop at his hip. Liora Quill had an empty cask lashed across her back, bung driven home and waxed, which made her clumsy at the gap in the Kettle Row wall and did not improve her temper about it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Inside the back room the silt had settled overnight. The bench of cracked glass stood as they had left it, and the strongbox hung on the oak post at chest height, four bolts through its back plate into the wood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory got the bar under the head of the lowest bolt and leaned. Nothing. He shifted his grip and leaned again, and the orange crust came away in a cloud, and the bolt turned a quarter and stopped. Above his head the boards of the ceiling were bowed down like a laden shelf, and that post was all that held them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora caught his wrist before the third pull and showed him the flat of her hand. Slowly. He nodded and worked the bar in small bites after that, a finger's width at a time, three bolts out and the fourth taking longer than the other three together. Maud hung back under the ceiling, both palms against the post, feeling for any give in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The last bolt came free into Jory's glove. The box dropped two inches and he had it, heavier than he had let himself expect, and the post stood where it was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They surfaced to breathe and went straight back down with the cask. Liora lashed it to the box, two turns and a hitch, and Maud hauled the knot tight with her heel braced on the floor. The cask took the weight and the box came up off the silt, swaying, and the three of them walked it through the black water towards the green smear of the gap.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It would not go. Jory turned it on its corner, scraping stone, and then it went, and the pull of the cask took it up the face of the wall faster than any of them could swim.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora broke the surface first and shouted, and Jory came up beside the hull with his hand already on the gunwale.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: It's up! Off your bow, Mr Ames, off your bow!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter Ames went down the length of his own boat in a way that would have worried his neighbours. He got both arms over the side and his hands under the cask, and Maud came up on the other side to counter him, and between them the strongbox came over the gunwale and landed on the wet boards with a sound that was all stone and no wood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It sat there dripping in the open morning. Harbour on all sides and nothing over it but sky.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: That's air. That's what she wanted. Nothing above it and nothing round it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter knelt on the boards and put the oilcloth down beside his knee. He wiped the plate clear with his sleeve, twice, and took the breath a man takes before he says the first of three things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he stopped, and leaned closer, and brought the loupe up to his eye.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The letters were gone. Jory had put his hand flat on those letters two days ago and felt every one of them stand proud under his glove. The plate was smooth now, smooth as a river pebble, and dark, and the water was running off it without beading.
